Whole-body tissue may mask tissue-specific signal; methylRAD gives low coverage; no paired gene expression. Uses the ambient-temperature subset of the Donelan et al. 2021 animals.

First demonstration that within-generation carryover scales to an ecosystem service, 1 year after a brief exposure.

Companion reproductive-endpoint paper (10.1016/j.scitotenv.2024.173569) reports F0 glycogen increase and higher 48 hpf reproductive success, plus F1 feminisation and accelerated gametogenesis.

column24: 3 replicate 37 L tanks per temperature condition, 10 adult urchins per tank (N=60 total)

column7: natural in-kelp vs outside-kelp variability in temperature, pH and dissolved oxygen during gametogenesis
column10: inside kelp forest (slightly elevated pH and temperature, more predictable low-frequency variability) vs outside kelp forest, Santa Barbara Channel

column20: within each larval pCO2 treatment, progeny from OUTSIDE-kelp-conditioned mothers had a 0.4 C higher LT50; larvae raised at high pCO2 (1053 uatm) were more susceptible to acute thermal stress regardless of maternal origin
column27: Natural conditioning contrast (field-conditioned mothers, not lab-dosed). Note the counterintuitive direction: mothers from the LESS buffered, less predictable outside-kelp environment produced the MORE thermally tolerant larvae, i.e. exposure to the more benign in-kelp refuge did not prime offspring.

column10: OA pH 7.77; OW +2 C (29 C); OAW +2 C and pH 7.77; vs ambient control

column20: larvae from OA and OAW parents were resilient to acidification and larvae from OW and OAW parents more tolerant of 29 C; BUT parental acclimation reduced larval arm lengths by as much as 21.4% and eggs were up to 21.8% smaller in females raised at 29 C
column27: Textbook TGP trade-off: stress tolerance gained at the direct cost of offspring size and maternal provisioning. First transgenerational climate-change study on a marine macroinvertebrate in which the F0 was acclimated across its whole reproductive life.

column7: ocean warming plus acidification (mid-century and end-century scenarios)
column10: two near-future scenarios (projected mid- and end-21st-century elevated temperature plus elevated pCO2) vs present-day ambient; exact set points not stated in abstract

column14: F1 reared 25 months under the same conditions; a natural selective pathogenic mortality event occurred at 10 months of F1 age

column20: Ambient-Ambient group was 21% larger and 31% faster in righting than all other groups; respiration depressed by 59% and righting slowed by 28% when parents came from near-future conditions; after the pathogen event size and respiration differences disappeared but a 29% righting deficit remained; spawning capacity 50% (ambient parents) vs 21% (other groups)
column27: MALADAPTIVE: significant NEGATIVE parental carryover effects, not acclimation. Physiological differences were erased by a selective mortality sweep while behavioural deficits persisted, i.e. decay was trait-specific. Assessments at 9, 10 and ~25 months.

column10: +2 C above ambient temperature and 940 ppm pCO2 vs present-day ambient
column11: more than 6 years total; F0 wild adults plus F1 and F2 larvae and adults continuously exposed

column18: F2 survivorship (>50% in all treatments) and test size; adult spawning performance; F3 larval arm and body length; F3 settlement success
column20: no size difference among treatment groups up to 720 d post-settlement; significant NEGATIVE relationship between number of generations exposed to future ocean conditions and spawning performance; larvae could only be raised from control or 0.5-generation-exposed adults; larvae from both parental groups only reached settlement when raised under control conditions; reduced arm length under climate-change conditions plus smaller arm and body lengths from climate-change parents
column27: MALADAPTIVE and CUMULATIVE: negative parental effects did not diminish across generations and for some traits INCREASED. Authors state explicitly that no evidence of transgenerational acclimation was detected. The most direct multi-generation refutation of assisted-conditioning optimism in an echinoderm. | PERSISTENCE SEMANTICS: this value is an exposure / tracking window under continuous or repeated conditioning, NOT days elapsed after conditioning ended. Do not rank it against clean-recovery-gap rows such as Drury_2022 or Lafont_2017.

column10: pH 7.7 and pH 7.4 vs control pH 8.0
column11: 2 months of parental exposure during gametogenesis
column14: sperm activated at pH 8.0, 7.7 or 7.4; larvae from each parental group reared at pH 8.0 or 7.7 for 20 days
column18: sperm motility, velocity, ATP content, ATP consumption, respiration rate; larval mortality; larval somatic growth
column20: POSITIVE carryover on sperm: velocity decreased more slowly and ATP content was higher in sperm developed under acidified conditions (longer sperm longevity); sperm motility and respiration unaffected. NEGATIVE carryover on larvae: reduced survival of larvae from pH 7.4 parents, with additive negative effects of parental plus larval low pH; larvae from low-pH parents showed NO increased capacity to cope with OA and all groups showed reduced somatic growth at low rearing pH
column27: Stage-dependent REVERSAL: the same parental conditioning benefited the gamete stage and harmed the larval stage. Direct counterexample to positive-TGP expectations in echinoids.

column10: acidified seawater vs control seawater (pH and pCO2 set points not reported in abstract)
column11: two-generation rearing experiment (exposure length not reported in abstract)
column14: larvae exposed to acidified seawater of the same pH as the parental treatment
column18: larval survival; larval body size; larval morphology
column20: larvae derived from parents acclimated to acidified seawater tended to have higher survival and showed less reduction in body size when exposed to the same pH, indicating a positive carry-over effect; no quantitative statistics in the abstract
column22: Partial (expression patterns of larvae from acclimated parents were substantially different from those of larvae from non-acclimated and control parents, but no quantitative overlap reported)
column27: Closed access; dose, exposure duration and replication were NOT extractable, which is a notable reporting gap for one of the few clearly POSITIVE echinoderm OA carryover results. Species is a commercial edible urchin in northern Japan.

column10: pH 7.72 / 1013 +/- 12 uatm pCO2 vs pH 8.06 / 412 +/- 6 uatm pCO2
column11: 2 months of adult conditioning at treatment pCO2 (preceded by 2 months acclimation to aquarium seawater; 4 months total in Menai Straits water before spawning)
column14: larvae spawned and reared at ~1000 uatm; separate acute heat shock of 25 C for 1 h applied to adults and to 2 and 4 dpf larvae
column18: larval transcriptome at 2, 3 and 4 dpf; HSP70 and HSP90 transcript induction by qPCR; larval morphometrics and abnormality rate
column20: larvae from low-pH-acclimated adults up-regulated antioxidants (glutathione-S-transferase family), CypP450 detoxification genes and small HSPs, i.e. maternal transcript pre-loading; larvae reared in low pH had 25-40% abnormalities and significantly smaller body length:width ratio (F=8.035, p=0.005); early larvae could not mount a full heat shock response (2 HSP transcripts up at 2 dpf, 5 at 4 dpf vs 8 in adults)
column22: Partial (transcriptional frontloading of antioxidants is concordant with previously reported improved larval performance under low pH, but larval morphology remained impaired)
column24: 5 females and 2 males successfully spawned per treatment with gametes pooled; 3 replicate larval cultures per treatment
column27: Mechanistic case for maternal pre-loading of protective transcripts. Caveat stated by the authors: the 2-month conditioning did NOT cover the whole reproductive cycle. Larval morphological impairment persisted despite the molecular priming.

column10: ~+3 C above ambient (21 C vs 18 C ambient/laboratory control)
column11: ~15 months of dam and sire exposure
column14: offspring reared at elevated (21 C) or ambient (18 C) temperature
column18: fertilization success; hatchability; larval survival; larval size traits; abnormality; metamorphosis
column20: no transgenerational effect on fertilization or metamorphosis; NEGATIVE transgenerational effects on hatchability and on most larval size traits; S. intermedius probably cannot achieve transgenerational acclimation to long-term elevated temperature for survival when offspring are also at elevated temperature; dam and sire effects were highly trait- and stage-dependent
column22: Discordant (companion transcriptome study on the same F0/F1 animals, Shi et al. 2020, 10.1038/s41598-020-64872-x, found 1891 DEGs from parental thermal history at ambient and 2203 at high developmental temperature, with 904 shared DEGs changing in the same direction and FEWER DEGs between developmental temperatures in embryos of warm parents - a molecular frontloading signature that maps onto WORSE performance)
column24: breeding design with multiple dams and sires (n per cross not stated in abstract); companion transcriptome used 3 biological replicates per group (12 mRNA libraries)
column27: MALADAPTIVE: explicit failure of transgenerational acclimation despite 15 months of parental conditioning. Valuable because it pairs a negative phenotype with a strong molecular response (see concordance field).

column7: maternal temperature shift timed to early vs late oogenesis

column11: thermal cue applied at either an early or a late stage of oogenesis (exact durations not stated in abstract)

column18: offspring upper and lower thermal tolerance limits measured at the adult stage
column20: EARLY-oogenesis cue: mothers produced offspring with greater cold AND heat tolerance whenever mother-offspring temperatures did NOT match (anticipatory maternal effect); LATE-oogenesis cue: more tolerant offspring when temperatures PERSISTED across generations; the maternal effect disappears as traits approach the upper sublethal and lethal limits
column24: reproductive pairs isolated in 20 ml glass bowls (n per treatment not stated in abstract)
column27: The single most important design lesson in this table: the DIRECTION of transgenerational plasticity reverses depending on the timing of the maternal cue within oogenesis. Also notable that the maternal effect persisted into the ADULT offspring stage, against the usual expectation that maternal effects fade early.

column7: ocean warming, ocean acidification, and their combination
column10: OW +3 C; OA pH -0.5 units; OWA +3 C and pH -0.5; vs control conditions
column11: full parental generation exposure across the life cycle
column14: F1 exposed to the same OW, OA or OWA conditions (trans-generational) vs F1 exposed with control parents (within-generational)
column18: fecundity; egg volume; juvenile growth rate; citrate synthase and electron transport system activity
column20: trans-generational OW exposure FULLY alleviated the within-generation reduction in fecundity and egg volume, accompanied by increased metabolic activity; within-generation OA reduced juvenile growth rates and egg volume, and trans-generational OA exposure alleviated the growth deficit but could NOT restore egg volume (mean egg volume still ~10% below control); OWA had no negative impacts either within- or trans-generationally
column24: n=12 replicate breeding pairs per treatment for fecundity
column27: Explicitly framed as a test of human-assisted trans-generational conditioning as a conservation/restoration and aquaculture tool. Authors' conclusion is the useful caution: trans-generational exposure does not always improve traits and may not be a universally useful tool.

column7: elevated temperature, and elevated temperature combined with elevated salinity
column10: 30 C (+3 C above the 27 C control) and 39 ppt elevated salinity vs control temperature and salinity; salinity alone was not tested

column14: F1 exposed to the same elevated-temperature or temperature+salinity conditions; reciprocal transplants at egg-mass vs juvenile stage
column18: juvenile growth rate; maximum body size; longevity; lifespan fecundity; citrate synthase and electron transport system activity
column20: trans-generation exposure restored 20% (elevated temperature) and 21% (temperature plus salinity) of lifespan fecundity; under temperature+salinity, worms transplanted at the egg-mass stage grew slower with lower energy-metabolism enzyme activity but reached a larger maximum body size and lived longer than those transplanted as juveniles; trans-generation elevated temperature created a trade-off in which slower-growing juveniles had greater lifespan fecundity
column27: One of very few marine-invertebrate designs that includes SALINITY conditioning. Only ~20% of the fecundity deficit was recovered, i.e. partial rescue at best. The TIMING of the transplant itself generated life-history trade-offs, so developmental window matters as much as dose.

column10: 26 ppt (low) vs 35 ppt (normal) seawater
column11: 2 weeks of adult exposure before reproduction; parents could be switched back and forth between salinities
column14: in vitro fertilization and larval rearing in matched vs mismatched salinity; larvae switched from natal to non-natal salinity immediately after fertilization or 2 or 4 days after fertilization, with survival scored 2 days after each switch
column18: sperm head area and tail length; egg morphology; fertilization success; larval survival
column20: both mothers and fathers adaptively adjusted gamete phenotype to maximise performance in the parental salinity regime; sperm from low-salinity fathers were much smaller while egg morphology did not change; STRONG performance trade-offs whenever gametes experienced a salinity that did not match the parents; larvae switched on the day of fertilization had the LOWEST survival and later switches progressively higher survival; the parental-environment effect persisted for the whole larval phase
column24: 4 tubs per salinity treatment; sperm from 3 males and eggs from 3 females pooled per assay
column27: Best available demonstration that conditioning MANUFACTURES phenotype-environment mismatch: conditioned larvae are effectively unable to disperse to non-natal salinities, so gamete plasticity becomes a source of reduced connectivity. Parents could reverse the gamete phenotype based on their most recent experience, i.e. the memory is short and rewritable.

column10: maternal colonies 300 ug/L Cu vs filtered seawater control; larvae subsequently 50 ug/L Cu vs filtered seawater control
column11: 6 h maternal exposure after larval release, then colonies returned to their field site to brood the test larvae
column14: larval copper exposure at 50 ug/L, then settlement and growth to maturity in the field with survival and growth tracked weekly for 6 weeks
column18: larval size at emergence; post-metamorphic survival; adult colony growth in the field
column20: in the population with NO historical copper exposure (Boat Ramp), maternal copper exposure had a strong NEGATIVE carryover effect on adult offspring growth and survival, worst when larvae were themselves also exposed; in the population WITH a copper history (Marina) there was little to no maternal or offspring treatment effect on adult growth and survival, and those parents produced larger larvae on average and increased larval size in response to copper; significant effect of population on F1 growth after 6 weeks in the field (LMM p<0.05)
column24: split-brood design across 2 populations with copper and control maternal treatments crossed with copper and control larval treatments (n per cell not extracted)
column27: MALADAPTIVE in naive populations: the direction of transgenerational plasticity is itself a locally adapted trait. Persistence figure is the 6-week post-settlement field tracking window; the interval between the end of maternal exposure and larval release (field brooding) was not resolved to days.

column10: copper exposure of maternal colonies vs toxicant-naive control (concentration not stated in abstract; cited by Neylan et al. 2022 as the basis for their 300 ug/L, 6 h protocol)
column11: laboratory copper exposure of maternal colonies followed by 1 week in the field to brood offspring
column14: offspring copper resistance assay, then 6 weeks in the field under low vs high intraspecific competition
column18: larval size; larval dispersal duration; larval copper resistance; post-metamorphic survival and performance
column20: offspring of toxicant-exposed mothers were LARGER, more dispersive and more copper-resistant than offspring of naive mothers; BUT maternal exposure history had pervasive NEGATIVE effects on post-metamorphic performance, particularly survival, after 6 weeks in the field, especially under high intraspecific competition
column27: The canonical stage-reversal / maladaptive result: conditioning improves performance in one life-history stage and reduces it in the next. Author's interpretation is that this cost is precisely why pollution resistance is INDUCED rather than constitutively expressed. Persistence figure combines the ~1 week brooding period and the 6-week field assessment.

column10: 100 ug/L Cu (as CuCl2.2H2O, Cu2+) vs artificial seawater control
column11: 6 h larval exposure
column14: transplantation of settled juveniles to 2 field sites in 2 seasons (winter and summer), with survival and growth followed for months
column18: larval attachment rate; metamorphosis success; post-metamorphic colony survival; colony growth
column20: Cu accelerated larval attachment in both seasons but inhibited metamorphosis; colony survival fell to about two-thirds of control in summer and to about 20% of control in winter; the survival decline occurred abruptly 3-5 weeks after exposure in summer and 14 weeks after exposure in winter, by which time colonies were 10-15 mm diameter (~100 zooids) and had undergone several budding cycles; surviving colonies grew more slowly than controls
column24: 2 seasons x 2 sites in SE Australia; transplanted colonies followed individually (n not extracted)
column27: BEST persistence-window dataset in this table and a strong maladaptive case: a 6 h larval exposure produced NO detectable survival effect for 3-14 weeks and then caused catastrophic mortality, with season setting the latency. Authors note this is far later than any previously reported carryover effect and that the larva could not have accumulated enough Cu in 6 h to affect all zooids directly, implying an inherited/propagated cellular lesion. Persistence recorded as ~21 d (earliest summer detection of the survival drop, 3-5 wk); the winter latency was ~98 d (14 wk), so season roughly quadrupled the delay before the carryover effect appeared.

column10: ~4 mg/L dissolved oxygen vs normoxic control
column11: from zygote to trochophore stage (duration in hours not reported in abstract)
column14: hypoxia tolerance assessment at the grow-out (juvenile) stage
column18: hypoxia tolerance; weight growth rate
column20: juvenile abalone exposed to hypoxia during early development were MORE hypoxia-tolerant but showed SLOWER weight growth - an explicit growth-versus-survival trade-off; no quantitative statistics available in the abstract
column22: Partial (carry-over phenotype attributed to strong selection on genes for signal transduction, autophagy, apoptosis and hormone regulation, plus long non-coding RNA regulation of DNA replication and repair, signal transduction, myocardial activity and hormone regulation)
column27: The only marine gastropod hypoxia-priming study located. Closed access, so exposure duration and persistence interval were not extractable. Important caveat: whole-genome resequencing showed strong SELECTION, so the authors cannot separate genetic selection from epigenetic carryover - this is differential survival as much as conditioning.

column7: nickel and ocean acidification, singly and combined
column10: Ni 6 ug/L; pCO2 1000 uatm; and their combination; vs control seawater
column11: six consecutive generations (F1-F6) of continuous exposure, followed by one generation (F7) in clean seawater
column14: one full generation of recovery in clean seawater (F7), with transcriptome compared against F6
column18: development; reproduction; survival; nickel accumulation; transcriptome
column20: Ni exposure compromised development, reproduction and survival across F1-F6, but ocean acidification ANTAGONISTICALLY alleviated Ni toxicity so that under combined exposure there was no disruption of Ca homeostasis and no inhibition of the calcium- or oxytocin-signalling pathways; the COST was a loss of transcriptome plasticity during recovery in F7, which limited the copepods' resilience when returned to their previous environment
column22: Partial (F6 within-generation and F7 recovery transcriptomes compared directly; no quantitative overlap figure extracted)
column27: Rare and highly relevant design: explicitly tests RECOVERY after multigenerational conditioning. The finding that multigenerational acclimation carried a hidden cost - reduced capacity to revert - is exactly the kind of latent maladaptive outcome this lab should flag.

column10: nanoplastics combined with ocean acidification vs control (nanoplastic concentration and pCO2 set points not reported in abstract)
column11: ten consecutive generations of multigenerational exposure, plus transgenerational groups returned to clean conditions
column12: F0 through F10 exposed, plus unexposed F1T and F2T transgenerational groups
column14: none (the F1T and F2T transgenerational groups were never themselves exposed to nanoplastics)
column18: reproduction (fecundity); gene-specific DNA methylation
column20: synergistic NEGATIVE effect of ocean acidification and nanoplastics on copepod reproduction across generations; reproductive impairment was still present in the F1T and F2T generations that had NEVER been exposed to nanoplastics
column22: Concordant (the intergenerational reproductive impairments were associated with differential methylation patterns of specific genes)
column27: MALADAPTIVE across an exposure gap: harm inherited by descendants that never met the stressor, with a methylation correlate. Closed access, so doses and the recovery interval in days were not extractable.

column10: pCO2 900 uatm and 1550 uatm vs 400 uatm control
column11: two full generations at the treatment pCO2
column14: reciprocal transplant of second-generation adults between pCO2 levels
column18: fecundity (egg production rate); respiration/metabolic rate
column20: second-generation adults showed a 29% decrease in fecundity at 900 uatm vs 400 uatm accompanied by a 10% increase in metabolic rate; reciprocal transplants showed that WITHOUT transgenerational effects fecundity would have fallen by as much as 67% at 1550 uatm; transgenerational effects held the loss at the 900-uatm level and removed the metabolic-stress signal, with respiration rates lower than at 900 uatm; the effect was fully reversible on transplant, i.e. phenotypic plasticity rather than fixation
column22: Discordant (the molecular companion study on the same two-generation experiment, De Wit et al. 2015, 10.1111/eva.12335, found genes involved in RNA transcription strongly DOWN-regulated in high-pCO2 lineages EVEN AFTER transplant back to control pCO2, plus 1513 of ~747,000 SNPs with consistent replicate frequency shifts in RNA transcription, ribosomal function, ion transport and oxidative phosphorylation - so the fecundity phenotype reversed but the transcriptome did not)
column24: 6 laboratory populations (2 replicate populations per pCO2 level)
column27: One of very few studies to QUANTIFY how much of an apparent OA effect is masked by transgenerational plasticity (67% predicted loss vs ~29% realised). Critical caveat from the companion paper: over two generations, plasticity and selection cannot be separated (estimated mortality >50% per generation), and the molecular state did NOT return to baseline even though the phenotype did.
